title: RFID Card Materials — From PVC to Paper
summary: PVC wins most RFID card jobs at $0.18-$0.32 per card: it's the cheapest option, prints beautifully and laminates happily with every inlay ever made. PET, PETG, PC and ABS buy more heat and chemical headroom — PC survives 10+ years — while wood and paper trade lifespan for compostability. Substrate drives 30-50% of per-card cost, so spec it next to the chip, not after the artwork.
heroPoints: PVC is the default winner: cheapest ($0.18-$0.32 per card at 5K-10K MOQ), prints like a dream and laminates happily with every inlay ever made. Most loyalty, event and hotel cards are PVC — and that's fine.
PET, PETG and PC are the durability upgrades: more heat, more chemical resistance, more money. PC is the bank vault of plastics — passports are made of it, and it holds up for 10+ years.

Wood and paper are the sustainability flex — gorgeous, compostable, and sprinters rather than marathon runners. Keep them away from hot laminators and puddles: paper retires within 6 months, wood veneer within 1-3 years.
imageAlt: Seven RFID card substrates lined up as a cascade of sheets — PVC, PET, PETG, PC, ABS, wood veneer and paper, each with a one-line personality — feeding into a single finished CR80 card, with a note that all seven look identical in the sample pack and stop being identical in a back pocket.

sections.title: Meet the seven RFID card materials: PVC, PET, PETG, PC, ABS, wood and paper
sections.intro: Seven substrates walk into a laminator. In the sample pack they look identical — then a back pocket, a squirt of hand sanitizer and a 150 °C printer head start telling them apart. Here's the roster: who survives, who thrives, and who quietly dissolves.

image.alt: Comparison matrix of the seven RFID card materials — PVC, PET, PETG, PC, ABS, wood veneer and paper — each with its nickname, best-fit applications, standout strength and one honest weakness, from the people's plastic to the single-use sprinter.

bullets: PVC (polyvinyl chloride) — the people's plastic. Cheap, cheerful and endlessly printable; it plays nicely with every printer and every inlay. Its one weakness: a splash of acetone or MEK and it goes to pieces. Best for loyalty, events and hotel keys.

PET (polyethylene terephthalate) — the sensible one. Shrugs off solvents and takes more heat than PVC without complaint. Slightly aloof: it wants a corona or plasma treatment before ink will fully commit. Best for transit and recycled (rPET) programs.

PETG — PET that went to finishing school. Glycol-modified PET: crystal-clear, tougher, and far friendlier on the laminator. Popular where you want PET's resilience but hate its printing tantrums. Best for durable ID and premium clear cards.

PC (polycarbonate) — the bank vault. Laser-engravable, borderline indestructible, happy from freezer to sauna: it's what passports and national IDs are made of, and your budget will feel it. Best for government ID and 10-year cards.

ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene) — the gym rat. Impact- and heat-tolerant to a toasty 80 °C, built for rough industrial handling and the occasional drop-kick. Prints fine, but warps if a retransfer printer runs too hot. Best for industrial and rugged access.

Wood veneer — the artisan. A whisper-thin real-wood veneer bonded to a PVC or PET core, preserving RF performance while delivering a distinctive tactile finish. Deeply allergic to hot laminators and long-term moisture. Best for luxury and premium NFC business cards.

Paper — the sprinter. Recycled or FSC-certified card stock with an embedded inlay: compostable, dirt-cheap and perfect for one-and-done jobs. Its final boss is, and always will be, a glass of water. Best for event badges and transit tickets.

sections.title: Why substrate material matters for RFID card performance
sections.intro: Every RFID card substrate looks like a reasonable choice in the sample pack. PVC, PET, ABS, a wood veneer that feels like the premium option — all of them photograph well and feel fine in the hand. They stop looking equivalent once they reach the field, where wallets, laminators and cleaning chemicals each get a vote. The substrate is not a cosmetic afterthought: it quietly decides four things that show up on your next reorder — RF transmission, mechanical durability, printing compatibility and end-of-life recyclability. Smart procurement teams spec the material right next to the chip and frequency, not as a footnote after the artwork is approved.

image.alt: Three-lane diagram of how a 13.56 MHz reader sees each card material: radio waves pass cleanly through PVC, PET, PETG, PC and ABS, take a minor dip through wood veneer, and detune 10-30% through genuinely soaked paper — recovering once it dries.

paragraphs: RF energy passes through different materials at different attenuation rates. A card substrate that absorbs or reflects 13.56 MHz energy reduces effective read range. PVC and PET are largely transparent to HF and UHF energy, while wood and paper introduce minor signal attenuation depending on moisture content and thickness. Only genuinely wet paper causes real read-range drama — and only until it dries.

callout.label: Material tip
callout.text: PVC remains the most cost-effective RFID card material; PET and PETG add chemical resistance, ABS handles extreme temperatures up to 80 °C — and if the card must survive a decade, that's polycarbonate territory.

sections.title: A "PVC card" is really a five-layer sandwich
sections.intro: When someone says "the material," they usually mean the two core sheets and the two protective overlays that get fused around the inlay. The chip and its antenna ride in the middle like the filling. Hot lamination fuses all five layers into a single 0.76 mm card — get the material wrong and this sandwich delaminates, usually right after deployment, never before.

image.alt: Exploded view of a laminated CR80 card: a clear overlay, a printed core sheet of PVC, PET or PC, the RFID inlay with antenna coil and chip in the middle, a printed back core and a clear sealing overlay — hot lamination fuses the stack into a single 0.76 mm card before die-cutting to CR80 size, 85.60 x 53.98 mm.

paragraphs: Every layer is a material decision: the overlays are clear PVC or PET, the core sheets carry the artwork, and the inlay in the middle doesn't care what it's wrapped in — as long as the lamination temperature suits the wrapper. That last clause is where wood and paper file their objections, as the next sections explain.

sections.title: How do mechanical and environmental durability by material work?
sections.intro: Polycarbonate survives a decade; paper is designed to be brilliant once. In between, lifespan tracks how much heat and chemistry a substrate can laugh off. A back pocket delivers temperature extremes, chemical exposure, UV radiation and mechanical flex all at once — the most honest accelerated-aging lab a card will ever see. Here's how the roster holds up.

image.alt: Horizontal bar chart of typical card lifespan in normal wallet and pocket use: PC 10+ years, ABS and PETG 5-8 years, PET 5-7 years, PVC 3-5 years, wood veneer 1-3 years and paper under one year.

paragraphs: Rule of thumb: the more heat and chemicals a material laughs off, the longer it lasts — and a five-year PVC card can quietly outlast a stack of paper cards that get replaced monthly.

sections.title: How do printing and personalization compatibility work?
sections.intro: Match the printing method to the substrate and you avoid the two most expensive words in card production: reprint everything. Each material has its own surface energy, heat tolerance and ink-adhesion mood, and those properties — not the artwork — decide which personalization methods are viable for custom-printed RFID cards.

image.alt: Selection guide matching four card printing methods to compatible materials: dye-sublimation to PVC, retransfer to PET, PETG and ABS, laser engraving to PC, PVC and ABS, and low-heat UV inkjet to wood veneer and paper.

paragraphs: PVC accepts dye-sublimation, direct-to-card thermal transfer, offset lithography and digital UV inkjet printing. PET requires corona or plasma surface treatment before ink adhesion is reliable for offset and screen printing. ABS is compatible with most thermal transfer ribbons but can warp under high-temperature retransfer printers. Wood and paper substrates are best suited for UV inkjet or screen printing where heat exposure is minimized.
bullets: Dye-sublimation on PVC produces photo-quality, edge-to-edge graphics — the gold standard for [hotel key cards](/solutions/hotel-key-cards/) and membership cards.
Retransfer (reverse-transfer) printing grips smooth-surface materials including PET, PETG and ABS beautifully, at a slightly higher cost per card.
Laser engraving on PC, PVC and ABS creates tamper-evident personalization that cannot be reprinted or altered — how secure IDs get personalized.
UV inkjet on wood and paper keeps the heat low and the veneer flat, and allows small-batch customization without tooling charges.

callout.label: Heads-up
callout.text: PET and PETG want a quick corona or plasma treatment before offset ink commits; ABS warps if a retransfer printer runs too hot; wood and paper curl when overheated. Send your printer make and model with the order and the factory ships blanks with the right surface treatment.

sections.title: What environmental and sustainability considerations apply?
sections.intro: "Eco" isn't a single ranking — it depends on whether you're optimising for recyclability, compostability or sheer longevity. Green procurement rules keep tightening and cards are an easy line item to clean up, but the honest comparison is over the card's whole life, not per unit. This is the part your ESG report cares about.

image.alt: Eco spectrum ladder running from harder-to-recycle to compostable: PVC at the top with chlorine and messy recycling, then ABS with limited recycling infrastructure, PC whose green argument is sheer longevity, PET in standard recycling streams, PETG and rPET with recycled content, FSC wood veneer with chain-of-custody, and compostable paper at the bottom.

paragraphs: PVC is the least environmentally favorable option due to chlorine content and difficulty of recycling post-consumer. PET and PETG recycle in standard plastics streams, and both come in recycled (rPET) grades. PC is recyclable and energy-intensive to make, but extremely long-lived — durability is its green argument. ABS has limited recycling infrastructure but is long-lived enough to offset replacement cycles. Wood and paper cards biodegrade naturally and are compostable if the embedded inlay is removed or uses biodegradable antenna materials.
bullets: Several European hotel chains now mandate PET or paper-based key cards to meet single-use plastics reduction targets.
Paper RFID cards with water-soluble adhesive allow inlay recovery and chip reuse at end of life.
FSC-certified wood veneer cards provide a verifiable chain-of-custody for sustainability audits.
The counter-intuitive bit: carbon-footprint comparisons should include card lifespan. A PVC card lasting five years may have lower lifecycle emissions than a paper card replaced monthly.

sections.title: How do chip and inlay compatibility across substrates work?
sections.intro: Not every chip format bonds reliably to every substrate. Wire-bonded inlays, flip-chip inlays and etched antennas each have different thermal and mechanical bonding requirements — and wood, in particular, has strong opinions about heat that a hot laminator simply does not share.
bullets: Plastics are easy: standard wet inlays (NTAG, MIFARE, DESFire) laminate happily between PVC, PET, PETG, PC and ABS layers using standard hot lamination at 120–150 °C.
Wood needs to stay cool: veneer cards require cold lamination or adhesive bonding to avoid scorching the veneer surface.
Paper too: inlays are cold-laminated or adhesive-mounted, since paper stock cannot withstand lamination temperatures above 100 °C.

Antenna material matters: aluminum-etched antennas on PET film are thinner and lighter than copper alternatives due to vapor deposition manufacturing, making them the dominant technology for cost-effective RFID inlays. Copper antennas offer higher conductivity and are preferred for performance-critical applications.
Prelams are a plastics club: pre-laminated inlay sheets are available in PVC and PET but not in wood or paper, so non-plastic substrates need manual inlay placement.

sections.title: Material price benchmarks and per-card cost build for 2026
sections.intro: Substrate selection drives 30-50% of the per-card cost in volume — and the entire reprint budget when you pick wrong. The benchmarks below are 2026 reference unit pricing for stocked RFID/NFC cards at 5K-50K MOQ, FOB China factory; aggregator/converter pricing in the US/EU adds 20-40% to these levels.

image.alt: Price ladder of 2026 per-card reference costs, FOB China factory: FSC paper with NTAG 213 cheapest, then standard PVC with NTAG 213, recycled PVC with NTAG 215, PET with MIFARE DESFire EV3 4K, and FSC wood veneer with NTAG 424 DNA at the premium end — with a note that the chip often moves the price more than the plastic.

bullets: Standard PVC + NTAG 213 — $0.18-$0.32 per card at 5K-10K MOQ; $0.12-$0.22 at 50K+ MOQ. The volume baseline; what most marketing-tap loyalty and event programs spec.
Recycled PVC (50-80% PCR) + NTAG 215 — $0.25-$0.45 at 5K-10K; $0.18-$0.32 at 50K+. Carries 10-15% premium over virgin PVC; pricing converges at 100K+.
PET (rPET or virgin) + MIFARE DESFire EV3 4K — $0.95-$1.65 at 5K MOQ; $0.65-$1.10 at 50K+. Hotels and transit migrating from MIFARE Classic 1K to DESFire EV3 hit this band.
FSC wood veneer + PVC core + NTAG 424 DNA — $1.50-$3.50 at 1K-5K MOQ; $0.85-$1.80 at 25K+. Premium brand-protection cards (LVMH Aura tier) and B2B networking metal-look NFC cards at the higher end.

FSC paper + NTAG 213 — $0.10-$0.22 at 5K-10K; $0.06-$0.14 at 50K+. Cheapest stocked option; 1-3 day production lead time when stocked. Single-use to short-lifecycle (event badge, transit ticket) only.
paragraphs: PETG typically sits a small step above standard PVC, and polycarbonate lands in the premium band near or above the PET/DESFire tier. With any of these, the chip usually moves the price more than the plastic — a DESFire or NTAG 424 DNA costs multiples of a basic NTAG 213.

sections.title: Card-body lamination, edge sealing and CR80 standard compliance
sections.intro: ISO 7810 ID-1 (the CR80 banking-card form factor — 85.60 x 53.98 mm, 0.76 mm thick) is the spec every standard RFID card must meet to fit existing card readers, ATMs, hotel-key locks and printer feeders. Miss it by half a millimetre and your beautiful card jams the very machines it was made for. Lamination process drives whether the card meets ISO 7810 + ISO 10373 flex/torsion durability tests.
bullets: Hot lamination (120-150 °C, 60-90 second cycle, Atlantek/Pollux/Kyodo Printing equipment) — produces edge-sealed CR80 cards with no delamination risk over 3-5 year lifecycle. Standard for PVC, PET and ABS bodies.

Cold lamination (room-temperature pressure-sensitive adhesive) — required for wood, paper and PLA substrates that warp at >100 °C. Edge-seal quality is lower; 2-3 year typical lifespan in regular pocket/wallet use.

Inlay placement tolerance — IDEMIA, IDP, Evolis, Zebra ZXP and Fargo card printers expect inlay coil at standard CR80 position (centered, 8-12 mm from card edge). Off-spec placement causes encoding failures at the printer head and very public first-deployment gremlins.

Edge-seal additives — BiFin, Toppan and Beijing Watchdata laminating compound provide UV-stabilised edge sealing that resists wallet-edge wear for 5+ years. Specify edge-seal grade in RFQ if cards face daily handling.

ISO 10373-1 flex test — 2,000 flex cycles for PVC, 3,000 for PET, 500-1,000 for wood/paper. Run cards through this test (Atlantek 510 or Mecmesin tester) before signing off on a 100K+ run; vendors with their own test labs should provide the report on request.

faq.question: Which RFID card material lasts the longest in harsh environments?
faq.answer: For a decade-plus lifespan and tamper resistance, polycarbonate (PC) is untouchable — it's why passports use it. For rugged industrial handling, ABS is the sweet spot of heat, chemical and impact resistance, with PET and PETG close behind on flex-cycle durability. PVC is adequate for indoor commercial use but degrades faster under UV exposure and solvent contact.

faq.question: Can wooden RFID cards be printed with full-color graphics?
faq.answer: Yes. UV inkjet printing allows full-color, photo-quality graphics on wood veneer surfaces. Laser engraving is also popular for a natural, premium aesthetic. Standard dye-sublimation printers cannot be used because the wood surface is not smooth enough for thermal transfer.

faq.question: When should I upgrade from PVC to PETG or PC?
faq.answer: Reach for PETG when you want PET-grade toughness and clarity without PET's printing fuss. Step up to PC when the card must survive 10+ years, resist tampering or carry laser-engraved security features — government ID territory. For everyday loyalty, event and hotel cards, PVC is cheaper and completely adequate.

faq.question: Are paper RFID cards reliable enough for commercial use?
faq.answer: Paper RFID cards are suitable for single-use or short-lifecycle applications such as event badges, transit tickets and promotional cards. They are not recommended for access control or membership cards that need to survive repeated handling over months or years. Paper's whole personality is "brilliant once, then retire."

faq.question: Does card material affect NFC read range?
faq.answer: Minimally. PVC, PET, PETG, PC and ABS are largely RF-transparent at 13.56 MHz. Wood and paper may reduce read range by 5–15 percent depending on moisture content and thickness, but the effect is negligible for tap-to-read applications where the card contacts the reader.

faq.question: How does the card material affect printer compatibility (Evolis, Zebra, Fargo, Magicard, Datacard)?
faq.answer: PVC, PET and ABS print cleanly on dye-sublimation printers (Evolis Primacy, Zebra ZXP Series 7/9, Fargo HDP5000, Magicard Ultima, Datacard CD800/SD460). Wood veneer and paper require either UV inkjet (Mimaki UJF-3042, Roland VersaUV) or pre-printed offset/digital cards delivered already-printed and laminated. Most printer manuals explicitly call out which card stock thicknesses (typically 0.30-0.84 mm) and surface treatments (varnish, hologram overlay, edge-to-edge print) are supported. Always send your supplier the printer make/model when ordering blanks so they can ship the correct surface treatment and inlay placement.

faq.question: Are there ISO 14443 / ISO 15693 certification differences across card materials?
faq.answer: The ISO 14443 / 15693 air-interface specifications are chip-and-antenna-level requirements that don't change with card body material. A NXP-certified MIFARE DESFire EV3 chip produces the same signal profile whether laminated into PVC, PET, ABS, wood or paper. Material affects mechanical durability (ISO 10373 flex/torsion), heat tolerance (ISO/IEC 7810) and printing compatibility — not the radio behaviour. The exception is heavy moisture absorption (paper soaked in water) which can detune the antenna by 10-30% — and it snaps right back once dry.
